WEEK 9 · RECORDING GUIDE · UNREAL 5.7.4

Master material first. Then the gallery.

A read-aloud walkthrough of the master material and all 23 gallery stations. Spend the most time tracing the master’s logic and testing its controls. Expand a refresher before recording whenever a mechanism needs clarification.

Target: 25:50 + navigation pausesMaster: 5:45 · full route: about 26–30 minutes

Project download · PowerPoint · PDF cheat sheet

Recording priority: Master material, five steps → gallery wall 01–21 → brief optional diagnostics 22–23 → close.

Protect the master walkthrough if time runs short. For the other stations, show the prepared comparison and use the short narration; live parameter edits are optional. The expandable refreshers are preparation notes, not extra timed sections.

Before recording

  • Work in a copy of the project. Open /Game/Week09/Maps/W09_MaterialGallery and let shaders finish compiling.
  • Start at Week 9 → Master material / separate reference area [Ref 14]. After its five steps, use the station cameras in wall order 01–23. Match each wall number with the menu’s bracketed Ref ID. Stop piloting before free camera movement.
  • Hide editor icons with G; use F11 if useful. Capture a short test with readable parameter names and clear audio.
  • Use static A/B specimens for most stops. Before any live edit, record the original value; duplicate and assign an instance when appropriate. Restore temporary tests afterward.
  • For burn: rehearse the PIE camera move to both burn benches, click the viewport, then use I / C / R. An editor-camera jump is not guaranteed to reposition the Play camera.
  • For post-process: pilot cameras 19, 20 and 21. For Star Nest: freeze both instances at the same time before comparing steps.
  • Record in short chapters. Hold the result for a moment before opening the graph. The times below budget narration and a short demonstration. Refresher reading and navigation pauses are additional.

Scope note: there is no completed Landscape station to tour. Texture arrays are an optional slide topic; the hands-on measured comparison belongs to Week 10. Basic diagnostics at the end get only a brief pass.

Master 1/5 · Read the parent and its instances

Say

These twelve specimens use the same opaque surface parent. An instance supplies different parameter values; the parent defines what those values actually do. Open the parent and you’ll see six output functions, with shared UV logic inside the texture functions. Double-click a function to follow the ordinary nodes inside it.

I would read this graph from a visible difference backward. For example, choose the polished and rough metal pair, find the roughness output, then trace its input and remapping controls. That is more useful than explaining every wire in order. The function boundaries tell us where to look without hiding how the material works.

Transition: Before looking at surface values, follow the coordinates shared by their textures.

Show / do

  1. Show the whole board, then open M_W09_SurfaceMaster. Point to its six output functions.
  2. Open MI_W09_05_PolishedMetal and MI_W09_06_RoughMetal from NotesMaster/Instances. Confirm the same parent.
  3. Double-click MF_W09_Roughness in the parent. Keep the preview and the relevant function visible.

/Game/Week09/NotesMaster/M_W09_SurfaceMaster · /Game/Week09/NotesMaster/Instances

Reset: Inspect the parent and functions without editing them; they are shared by the instances.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Trace it
Assigned instance → parent → output function → source texture/parameter. Use a visible difference to choose the output to inspect.
Three different jobs
The parent defines the surface logic. Functions package reusable logic. Instances override exposed values without copying the graph.
Check your understanding
Why do .12/.12 and .70/.70 look different with the same parent? Their roughness remap endpoints differ; the graph itself is shared.

This is an opaque Default Lit surface parent. Glass, post-process, dissolve and foliage use their own suitable parents. Functions organize logic; they do not prove lower GPU cost.

1:20–2:30 target · Ref 14 · PRIORITY · same master board

Master 2/5 · Shared UVs and feature switches

Say

Every texture function uses the same UV transform, so color and surface detail stay aligned. In the simple branch, UVTile multiplies both coordinates. In the advanced branch, one four-component parameter stores U and V scale, followed by U and V offset. These are numbers, even though Unreal displays the parameter using a color-style editor.

The formula is UV times scale, plus offset. UseAdvancedUV selects which branch is compiled. Turning the override checkbox on lets this instance override the inherited switch; the switch’s value is the separate choice of branch. If I edit the advanced vector while the simple branch is active, I should not expect a visible change.

Transition: Now we can adjust the surface response without losing texture alignment.

Show / do

  1. Open MF_W09_UV. Trace UV0 → scale → offset → UseAdvancedUV.
  2. Open MI_W09_03_Brick_UV: UseAdvancedUV is on; UVScaleOffset is (2, 1, .25, .1). Point to all four numeric components.
  3. Compare with MI_W09_02_Brick_ORM. If demonstrating a live change, use a duplicate and change only U scale before restoring it.

/Game/Week09/NotesMaster/Functions/MF_W09_UV · Instances/MI_W09_03_Brick_UV

Reset: Restore the edited vector and switch. Static-switch changes can compile; wait for completion before judging the preview.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
Simple: UV0 × UVTile. Advanced: UV0 × (R,G) + (B,A), from UVScaleOffset.
Concrete values
(2,1,.25,.1) repeats U twice, leaves V scale at one, and offsets U by .25 and V by .1. The same transform reaches the surface textures.
If nothing changes
Enable the parameter override and UseAdvancedUV. In advanced mode, the uniform UVTile value is bypassed. Treat the vector numerically; alpha is the fourth control, not opacity.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Advanced mode replaces the uniform UVTile branch; UVTile is not an additional multiplier in that mode.

2:30–3:45 target · Ref 14 · PRIORITY · same master board

Master 3/5 · Trace useful surface controls

Say

Roughness is remapped between two endpoints. A dark texture value selects the low endpoint, a light value selects the high endpoint, and intermediate values interpolate. Equal endpoints remove the texture’s variation and give constant roughness. That is how the polished and rough metal pair isolates one useful difference.

The base-color function has a deliberate order: brightness, saturation, a bounded power curve, then tint. ColorPower is not symmetric contrast; it bends the tonal values. I’d change one control at a time and watch which property changes. The point of the master is that each control has a predictable job, not that every option should be enabled on every surface.

Transition: The packed-map switch changes both the texture source and the controls that drive some outputs.

Show / do

  1. Compare MI_W09_05_PolishedMetal (.12/.12) with MI_W09_06_RoughMetal (.70/.70). Both are metallic, with the same tint.
  2. In MF_W09_Roughness, show texture signal → Lerp endpoints → Saturate → Roughness. Use the separate branch for this comparison.
  3. Open MI_W09_04_Brick_Tint and MF_W09_BaseColor. Trace the processing order; use a duplicate for any isolated brightness or saturation test.

/Game/Week09/NotesMaster/Functions · MF_W09_Roughness / MF_W09_BaseColor

Reset: Keep the staged pairs intact. Restore edited controls on the duplicate or restore the original assignment.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Roughness
saturate(lerp(low, high, map)). If low=.2 and high=.8, a map value of .5 produces .5. Equal endpoints ignore map variation. Reversed endpoints invert the response.
Base color
Brightness → Desaturation using 1−Saturation → bounded Power → Tint → clamp. With a neutral tint, all four controls at 1 preserve the sampled base color.
Metal / specular
Separate mode: IsMetal off gives 0; on gives 1 unless HasMetallicTexture selects its R channel. OverrideSpecular off gives .5; on uses a clamped blend from BaseSpecular toward 1.
Only if needed
NormalStrength is the existing detail-strength control. AO uses lerp(1, AO, strength), so strength 0 returns white and disables material AO; multiplying AO by zero would do the opposite. Visibility depends on lighting/rendering.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Skip a standalone normal-map explanation. The normal, AO and specular controls are available as targeted diagnostics in the refresher below.

3:45–5:05 target · Ref 14 · PRIORITY · same master board

Master 4/5 · Separate maps versus packed ORM

Say

Compare the separate brick instance with the packed ORM instance. The intended surface stays consistent while three scalar maps share one RGB texture: red is ambient occlusion, green is roughness, and blue is metallic. That channel agreement is a contract between the texture and the graph.

UsePackedORM also selects packed-mode controls. With it enabled, roughness uses ORM_MinRoughness and ORM_MaxRoughness; AO uses ORM_AOStrength. The separate-map controls are bypassed. This is a common reason a slider seems broken. Packing is useful for organizing and sampling compatible data, but the filename alone tells us nothing about the channel order, and this comparison is not a performance measurement.

Transition: Finish the master walkthrough with a repeatable way to test a change.

Show / do

  1. Compare MI_W09_01_Brick_Separate and MI_W09_02_Brick_ORM. Verify UsePackedORM off versus on.
  2. Open ORMTexture, inspect R/G/B individually, then trace those channels to AO / roughness / metallic functions.
  3. On a duplicate of the packed instance, enable the override checkboxes for ORM_MinRoughness and ORM_MaxRoughness; set both to .15, then both to .70. Compare under the same light.

/Game/Week09/NotesMaster/Instances · MI_W09_01_Brick_Separate / MI_W09_02_Brick_ORM

Reset: Restore the duplicate’s roughness endpoints and assignment. Keep the original separate/packed pair unchanged.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Channel contract
ORM R → AO; G → roughness; B → metallic. UsePackedORM switches all three paths together. Confirm the actual texture channels before assigning a different pack.
Active controls
Separate: MinRoughness / MaxRoughness / AOStrength, plus IsMetal and HasMetallicTexture. Packed: ORM_MinRoughness / ORM_MaxRoughness / ORM_AOStrength, with metallic read from B.
Common trap
A checked scalar override still has no effect if its branch is bypassed. Change packed controls in packed mode, and keep the data texture linear.
What packing buys
Three compatible scalar signals can share an RGB texture and coordinates. Actual cost depends on sampling, format, resolution and use; inspect/profile the compiled material rather than counting function boxes.
Reference view + explanation boundary

ORM is linear data; base color remains separate. Later, brick POM uses MRAH: R metallic, G roughness, B AO, A height. No height input is sampled by this master.

5:05–6:05 target · Ref 14 · PRIORITY · same master board

Master 5/5 · Make one change and diagnose it

Say

For a controlled experiment, duplicate an instance, assign that duplicate to one specimen, and change one value with a clear prediction. If nothing happens, check the assignment, the override checkbox, and the branch selected by the static switch. Then trace the control to the output you expected to change.

Changing a parameter on this instance is different from editing a shared function. A shared function edit can affect every material that uses it. For runtime animation, a dynamic material instance can change scalar and vector parameters, but it still has to be assigned to the component. A static switch is a compiled feature choice, not a control to animate every frame.

Transition: The gallery starts by extending that ownership question: which controls affect one object, and which affect many?

Show / do

  1. Use the packed roughness duplicate from the previous chapter; show its assignment in the mesh’s material slot.
  2. Point to the enabled scalar override and UsePackedORM branch. Predict smoother versus rougher before showing the result.
  3. Restore the original material slot and return to the board. Then jump to gallery wall 01 / Ref 11.

/Game/Week09/NotesMaster/Instances · duplicate a reference instance in the recording copy

Reset: Restore the original material assignment. Do not save experiments over the reference parent, functions or staged instances.

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Fast diagnosis
1. Correct instance assigned? 2. Override checked? 3. Correct static branch? 4. Shader compilation finished? 5. Camera/light able to reveal the property?
Useful prediction
Both roughness endpoints at .15 should give a smoother response than both at .70. If the result retains map variation, first check the active mode and control names.
Scope of an edit
An instance value affects users of that instance. A parent/function edit can affect many instances/materials. A dynamic instance must be assigned before its runtime parameters can affect the mesh.

01 · Shared and per-object controls

Say

These three surfaces separate shared settings from per-object data. A material parameter collection is a common source: changing a value affects every material that reads it. Custom Primitive Data lives on a mesh component, so one component can supply a different color without needing a separate material for every object. Before changing a value, identify where it lives and which objects are supposed to respond.

Transition: Next, the same idea of scope applies to coordinates: does the texture live on the mesh or in the world?

Show / do

  1. Frame all three spheres. In MPC_11_SharedControls, compare SharedRoughness .2 and .8, then restore the baseline.
  2. Select one sphere’s mesh component and point to Custom Primitive Data entries 0–2 for RGB. One color edit is enough.

/Game/Week09/ReferenceSystems · MPC_11_SharedControls / M_11_SharedAndPerObject

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
MPC_11_SharedControls supplies SharedRoughness to all readers. Custom Primitive Data entries 0–2 supply RGB on each individual mesh component.
Test
Change only SharedRoughness: all reader specimens should respond. Restore it, then change one component’s RGB: that component should differ.
Common confusion
An instance parameter, a collection parameter and per-component data have different owners. Duplicating an instance does not give it a private copy of the collection.

7:05–7:45 target · Ref 05

02 · World-aligned projection

Say

The objects have different dimensions, but the texture is sampled in world space. That lets us keep a consistent feature size without relying entirely on each mesh’s UV layout. The tradeoff appears when an object moves: the world-space texture field stays put, so the surface can appear to move through it. World projection is useful when that behavior matches the job, rather than being a universal replacement for UVs.

Transition: Now we’ll replace a coordinate-based decision with a painted control signal.

Show / do

  1. Compare the brick scale across the shapes.
  2. If useful, translate one mesh a small distance, show the pattern staying in world space, then undo the movement.

Select a specimen → Details → Materials → assigned world-projection material

Reset: Undo only your test movement; verify the original transform.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
World position supplies projection coordinates, so the texture has a size in world units rather than being stretched by each object’s UV layout.
Test
Translate a specimen a little, then undo. The world texture field stays fixed while the mesh moves through it.
Common confusion
Projection solves a coordinate-placement problem. It does not automatically solve moving-object anchoring or every visible seam.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Do not imply that world projection follows a moving object automatically.

03 · Vertex paint and height blend

Say

The first object reveals the stored vertex colors. Those values interpolate across the mesh and become inputs to the material. The next comparison uses painted weights to mix surfaces; the height-based version reshapes the transition using height information. The important difference is the boundary, not added geometry. Vertex density limits the detail you can paint, and the material decides what each color channel means.

Transition: Paint gives us authored placement. A direction can give us procedural placement.

Show / do

  1. Show the painted-weight diagnostic, ordinary blend and height-blend specimen.
  2. Open MI_08_HeightBlend; compare Blend Contrast 1 and 4 with paint and textures fixed. Point to the boundary.

/Game/Week09/ReferenceSystems/MI_08_HeightBlend

Reset: Restore recorded Blend Contrast (staged 2). Avoid repainting the saved examples during the take.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
Painted vertex values interpolate across the triangles. The ordinary blend uses those weights directly; the height blend reshapes the transition with height detail.
Why the edge differs
The broad painted region decides where the blend happens; height information affects which fine details appear first along the boundary.
Check
Hold paint and textures fixed; change Blend Contrast. The edge should change while the mesh silhouette does not. Inspect the parent: ordinary blend uses R=stone/G=sand, while this height example uses R.
Reference view + explanation boundary

The regular blend uses R=stone and G=sand; the height blend uses R as its blend control. Check the parent before painting.

8:50–9:30 target · Ref 09

04 · Directional coverage

Say

Here the material compares the surface direction with a chosen world-space direction. Faces pointing toward that direction receive more coverage. That is why snow can favor upward-facing areas, while moss can use a different directional bias. The surface vector and comparison direction have to use the same coordinate space. The mask then controls where one surface contributes over another.

Transition: The rock example makes that coverage easier to read on an irregular surface.

Show / do

  1. Compare the neutral, world-up snow and directional moss examples.
  2. Open MPC_09_Directions to show Snow_Direction and Moss_Direction; changing a direction is optional.

/Game/Week09/ReferenceSystems/MPC_09_Directions

Reset: Restore any edited vector. Snow expects a unit direction; use a nonzero direction for moss.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
Compare the surface direction with a selected direction in the same coordinate space, then shape that agreement into a coverage mask.
Interpret it
High agreement means facing the chosen direction. World-up coverage should favor top-facing areas even when the mesh is rotated.
Check
Changing Snow_Direction is shared through the collection. Restore its unit vector; use a nonzero moss direction. This is a placement rule, not weather simulation.
Reference view + explanation boundary

This is a coverage rule, not a simulation of weather or accumulation.

05 · Snow on rock

Say

This is the same rock shown bare, with snow, and with its coverage mask exposed. White in the mask selects snow; black keeps the rock. Direction gives us the broad placement, while texture detail breaks up the boundary. Because the underlying materials include surface detail, the coating reads as more than a flat color change. Previewing the mask is the fastest way to understand why a particular area is covered.

Transition: Directional coverage acts across a surface. Decals let us place a more localized change.

06 · Decal receivers

Say

A decal is a projected contribution to another surface. It can change roughness or other supported material properties without adding a new visible object. Compare the dry receiver, the roughness response, the puddle and the angle mask. If a decal seems invisible, first check where it projects and whether the receiver accepts the relevant data. A roughness-only change needs useful reflected light; it may not create a color patch.

Transition: The next display gives that wet response a clearer lighting reference.

Show / do

  1. Show the four labeled receiver comparisons.
  2. Select the roughness decal and its instance. Compare Roughness .03 and .8 from the same view; show projection bounds briefly.

/Game/Week09/ReferenceSystems/MI_10_RoughnessDecal

Reset: Restore the recorded roughness and assignment. Keep camera and lighting fixed for the comparison.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Signal
The projector writes decal data where its volume intersects receiving surfaces. The receiver decides which supported material channels contribute.
Two receiver controls
Receives Decals is on the mesh component. Decal Response is on the receiver material. Projection bounds, accepted channels and lighting all matter.
Manual DBuffer case
For a receiver explicitly applying DBuffer data itself, set automatic Decal Response to None to avoid double application. Do not copy that setting to ordinary receivers expecting automatic response.
Test
Compare .03 versus .8 roughness from a fixed view with visible reflections. A roughness-only decal can work correctly without changing the surface’s base color.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Actor Receives Decals and material Decal Response are different controls. Manual DBuffer blending requires deliberate receiver setup; avoid applying the contribution twice.

07 · Puddles and reflected light

Say

Watch the reflected strip light rather than looking only for a darker patch. The comparisons separate a dry surface, a smoother response and a wet patch with both surface and color changes. The wet region is convincing because those cues agree. This is also why a shader can look unconvincing in an empty test scene: without something useful to reflect, the roughness difference is much harder to judge.

Transition: A second reflective layer can also be part of the surface itself, as in clear coat.

Show / do

  1. Frame the dry, smooth and wet plates together. Hold long enough to compare the light strip.
  2. Move the camera slightly to show the view-dependent reflection; point out the boundary and surface detail.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

What changes
The wet patch combines a local surface response with a color change. Its flatter/smoother response makes the strip-light reflection read differently from the dry textured surface.
How to read it
Track the reflected light across dry, smooth and wet specimens. Then shift the camera slightly; reflections depend on view direction.
Common confusion
A darker patch alone reads like a stain. A smooth patch without reflected features can be hard to see. This example needs both the receiver and the studio lighting.
Reference view + explanation boundary

08 · Clear coat

Say

Clear coat adds a separate smooth specular response over the underlying material. Here we keep the textured wood recognizable and compare the coating contribution. The goal is to distinguish the top response from the base surface, rather than simply making everything uniformly shiny. This is useful for varnish, automotive paint and other layered finishes where one roughness value cannot describe the whole appearance.

Transition: Now let’s separate that visual idea of a coating from the way reusable material layers are organized.

Show / do

  1. Compare the coat-off and coat-on specimens from the same angle.
  2. Open M_ClearCoatStudy and point to the coat contribution alongside the underlying surface attributes.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Meaning
Clear Coat is a shading-model response for a coat over a base surface. The base still contributes beneath the coat.
Test
Compare the coat-off/on specimens with the same wood detail and view. Identify the additional coat response rather than judging only overall brightness.
Keep separate
Clear Coat is not the Material Layers asset workflow. One describes a shading response; the other organizes reusable material attributes and blends.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Clear coat is a shading-model feature. It is not the same feature as Unreal’s native Material Layers workflow.

12:40–13:30 target · Ref 12

09 · Native Material Layers

Say

This display uses reusable surface layers and a separate blend definition. A layer supplies attributes such as color, roughness and normal; the blend decides how another layer contributes. The three instances show different transition settings. Keeping the layer definition separate from its blend makes the material easier to reuse. When editing a layered instance, the parameter’s association and layer index matter as well as its name.

Transition: The wood-and-paint example makes the contribution of each layer more explicit.

Show / do

  1. Compare the three staged transitions: .25, .5 and .75.
  2. Open MI_12_Layers_1 → Layer Parameters. Locate blend-associated Transition at index 0.

/Game/Week09/ReferenceSystems · MI_12_Layers_0 / MI_12_Layers_1 / MI_12_Layers_2

Reset: If you change Transition, restore the value for that same blend association and index.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Three pieces
A Material Layer outputs surface attributes; a Material Layer Blend combines the lower/upper results; the parent’s Material Attribute Layers node evaluates the stack.
Where to edit
Open the instance’s Layer Parameters. Transition belongs to blend index 0, not a global parameter with the same name.
Test
Compare staged Transition .25 / .5 / .75, then inspect which blend owns that value. The next wood/paint station makes the same structure easier to read.
Keep separate
An ordinary Lerp or BlendMaterialAttributes can mix surfaces without using this native layer-stack workflow. Stacking attributes does not stack extra geometry.
Reference view + explanation boundary

This is native Material Layers. An ordinary Lerp or material-attribute blend can layer appearances without using this asset/instance system.

10 · Wood and paint coating

Say

Read this comparison as bare wood, partial paint and full paint. The coverage control chooses where the paint layer replaces the wood attributes. Color, roughness and normal response change together, which is why the coated region can look smoother rather than merely tinted. This particular mask is a UV ramp. It makes the blend easy to inspect, but it is not claiming that paint is accumulating in the wood’s height details.

Transition: Next we’ll compare surface blending with a technique that changes the apparent depth of texture detail.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Actual stack
ML_DarkBase supplies the textured wood surface; ML_BlueCoating supplies paint; MLB_CoatingCoverage decides where paint replaces wood attributes.
Mask mechanism
At 0 coverage the mask is all base; at 1 it is all coating. Between them, a sharpened UV.y threshold moves a boundary across the sample.
Why this is not just tint
The mask changes color, roughness and normal response together. Partial coating should preserve visible wood on one side and a smoother painted response on the other.
Test
CoatingCoverage lives on blend index 0. Compare 0 / .5 / 1 with the same lighting. This mask uses UV position, not wood height or simulated paint deposition.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Mixing attributes does not add physical coating geometry. This example uses a UV coverage mask, not height blending.

14:25–15:05 target · Ref 04

11 · BumpOffset and parallax

Say

These planes use the same texture set, so the useful comparison is how the detail responds when the camera moves. BumpOffset shifts the texture lookup; parallax occlusion mapping searches through a height field for a stronger depth illusion. Both operate on the appearance of the existing surface. Check the outer edge of the plane as well as the detail inside it: apparent relief does not mean the mesh gained that geometry.

13 · Foliage wind / WPO

Say

The first clump is still, the second moves, and the third reveals the root-to-tip weight. World Position Offset changes the positions of existing vertices. Multiplying the motion by this weight keeps the roots anchored while the tips bend. A time signal and spatial variation keep the motion from feeling completely uniform. The key is to make the main bend read clearly before adding more layers of noise.

Transition: Flow changes something different: the direction of sampled detail across a surface.

Signal
Time and position create a varying sway; a root-to-tip weight multiplies it before the offset reaches WPO.

16:55–18:00 target · Ref 18

14 · Flow direction and flow mask

Say

Read these four views as a uniform pan, direction-driven flow, direction plus a mask, and the mask by itself. The red and green channels encode a two-dimensional direction. Here the blue channel is a separate influence mask. Direction answers which way; the mask answers where and how much. Two offset animation phases blend across the reset so the pattern does not simply snap back in one obvious loop.

Transition: A shared control signal can also coordinate several outputs, which is what the burn example does.

Show / do

  1. Let the four specimens animate for a few seconds; point out where the masked result slows or stays still.
  2. Open M_FlowStudy and show Field.rg * 2 - 1, the independent B influence, and the two-phase blend. If needed, change Speed only.

/Game/Week09/AdvancedStudies · M_FlowStudy / MI_Flow_Pan / MI_Flow_Direction / MI_Flow_Masked / MI_Flow_Mask

Reset: Restore Speed (staged .25) and leave the four Mode values 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 intact.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Decode direction
RG is stored in 0–1 and decoded with RG × 2 − 1. A value of .5 becomes zero; values on either side encode opposite directions. Vector length also affects the offset unless normalized.
Separate influence
B is the scalar influence: zero stops the local UV offset and one gives the full directed offset. It is neither a third direction axis nor an opacity mask here.
Why two phases
Two repeating offsets are half a cycle apart. Crossfading hides the reset of one while the other is visible. A single steadily stretched lookup would eventually become visibly distorted or reset.
Test
Compare pan → RG direction → direction × B → B diagnostic. At black in B, the masked sample’s offset is zero. Speed changes the shared animation rate, not the mesh.
Reference view + explanation boundary

The flow texture is linear data. This moves sampled detail; it does not move the mesh or simulate fluid.

Blueprint drives the demonstration over time, while the material turns those controls into appearance.

The shield comparison separates the base surface, contact response and an expanding impact ring. For the ring, distance from an impact position becomes a band whose radius changes with age. Its intensity fades over that lifetime. The material can visualize an event, but gameplay still has to provide the event’s position and timing. The repeating hit here is a preview loop, so it should not be mistaken for a completed collision-driven interaction system.

22:20–23:30 target · Ref 25

20 · GLSL → HLSL / Star Nest

Say

This is a manageable shader-port example because it uses one image pass, with no input textures or feedback buffers. UV coordinates, time and a few controls enter an HLSL Custom node, and its color drives an unlit material’s emissive output. Porting means matching the inputs and mathematical behavior, not just renaming vector types. We freeze time to compare step counts fairly; a prettier screenshot alone does not tell us the GPU cost.

Transition: Finally, a material can operate on the rendered image instead of one surface in the scene.

Show / do

  1. Set UseFrozenTime=1 and FreezeTime=10 on both 8-step and 20-step instances, then compare.
  2. Open M_StarNest_Port. Point to UV / Time → Custom → Emissive. Mention vec3→float3, mix→lerp, fract→frac; mod and matrix order need care.

/Game/Week09/AdvancedStudies · M_StarNest_Port / MI_StarNest_8Steps / MI_StarNest_20Steps

Reset: Restore UseFrozenTime=0 for animation; retain the separate VolumeSteps values 8 and 20.

Refresher · mechanism, test and common confusion

Read before the take; these notes are outside the timed narration.

Porting route
Identify source inputs and passes → supply equivalent UV/time inputs → translate GLSL math to HLSL → send the resulting color through Custom to Emissive → compare at fixed time.
Small translation examples
vec3 becomes float3; mix becomes lerp; fract becomes frac. GLSL mod(x,y) uses x−y×floor(x/y), which differs from fmod for some negative values. Check matrix order rather than doing blind text replacement.
Why this source fits
The selected port is one pass with no input textures or feedback buffers. That avoids having to recreate an entire multipass rendering pipeline.
Check
Freeze both instances at time 10 before comparing 8 and 20 steps. More detail is an appearance observation; target-hardware GPU cost needs its own measurement.
Reference view + explanation boundary

The source license is included in SourceArt/StarNest. This is a procedural fractal starfield, not a cloud simulation; no target-machine timing claim is made.

These camera presets use a post-process material to treat the rendered scene image. The watercolor-inspired view combines color grouping, a wash, grain and an edge treatment. Ink emphasizes edges and reduces saturation; posterization uses fewer color steps. These are parameter choices in the same small system. Because the effect is attached to the camera, piloting the correct camera matters: selecting a normal gallery view will not show the same treatment.

Signal
The rendered scene color enters a post-process material. Its parameters change the image after the scene surfaces have been rendered.
Controls
Strength blends original and treated image. PigmentSteps controls grouping, Saturation affects color, PaperGrain adds image texture, Wash shifts toward a paper tone, and EdgeInk darkens detected image variation.
Important boundary
This compact study uses image-color variation for edges; it is not a semantic object-outline system or a physically simulated watercolor medium.
Check
Pilot the watercolor, ink and poster cameras individually. If the style disappears after leaving pilot, that is consistent with the effect being camera-bound. Restore each preset after comparison.
Reference view + explanation boundary

Controls: Strength, PigmentSteps, PaperGrain, EdgeInk, Wash and Saturation. This is a compact stylization study, not a full painterly-rendering pipeline.
